england-tuchel-alexander-arnold.headline: England player ratings and Tuchel's Alexander-Arnold question
england-tuchel-alexander-arnold.body_md:
Trent Alexander-Arnold got his chance in Prague on Tuesday and took it. He made one decisive pass in a 2-0 Nations League win over Czechia. Whether that changes anything for Thomas Tuchel's right flank is a separate question, and the England manager was careful not to answer it.

The full-back was recalled on 18 September, his first call-up since the World Cup and his first England start under Tuchel. He had not played for England since 2025. Tuchel's message on recalling him was blunt: "It's an opportunity for Trent", and it was "now time to fight for his place".

## One pass, and an early red card

The decisive moment came two minutes after the break. Alexander-Arnold's right-foot delivery found Anthony Gordon for the opening goal, and Harry Kane added the second. Czechia were down to ten men after an early red card for Pavel Sulc, which flatters any attacking rating on the night.

The marks were generous all the same. Sports Illustrated gave him 8.4 and called the delivery "a cross of the highest quality". Goal.com scored him 8 and said that in his hybrid role he was the main architect of England's attacking shape. A more cautious 7 came from JingleTree, which noted he had little to do defensively.

That caveat matters. The question about Alexander-Arnold has never really been whether he can pass. It is what happens when the opposition has the ball and the space behind him is exposed. A side playing with ten men for most of the evening did not test that.

Tuchel was measured afterwards. He told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He did very well. He had an excellent assist. Overall, like everyone, he was professional, top attitude and one decisive action." That is praise for the assist and the attitude, and it stops short of endorsing him as first choice.

Gordon was warmer: "Only a certain number of players have that ability, technique and bravery to make that pass... I've been dying to play with him." Alexander-Arnold himself said: "The manager gave me a chance, now hopefully he is happy."

## A position still unsettled

The BBC's analysis argues that it is time for Tuchel to show more trust. It puts the numbers starkly. Alexander-Arnold is reported to be Tuchel's ninth right-back in 24 games, though the tally is the BBC's and depends on how a hybrid role is counted. Whatever the exact figure, a manager who has rotated that many players through one position has not found the answer.

The pattern points to a settled hesitancy rather than a single bad night. Tuchel left Alexander-Arnold out for more than a year while favouring other options. He has now brought him back on probation, not on merit. One assist against ten men does not overturn that approach, and the manager's careful wording suggests it has not.

The counter-argument is that Alexander-Arnold's qualities are scarce. England have creators in abundance, and few of them can switch play or split a defence from deep as he can. Selecting him means building the defence around him, which is the trade-off Tuchel appears reluctant to commit to.

## What next

The next Nations League window will show whether the Prague performance was an audition or the start of a run. A start against opposition at full strength, with no red card to help, would be the real test. Until then the right-back position stays open, and Alexander-Arnold is still fighting for it.

man-city-findings-fallout.headline: How Man City's financial arrangements unravelled, and how football is reacting
man-city-findings-fallout.body_md:
Manchester City have been found to have broken the Premier League's financial rules on a scale that has no precedent in English football. An independent commission has upheld 114 of the 115 charges brought against the club. The findings cover the nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, when City rose from mid-table ambition to domestic dominance under Abu Dhabi ownership. No punishment has been set, and City say they will appeal.

The verdict concerns football, but it also tests a wider question. Can an industry that writes its own rules, relies on its members to report their own numbers and then polices itself do the job credibly?

## What the commission found

The commission found that City's revenues were inflated, and their costs understated, by more than £900m across the period. The aim was to make the club look compliant with the league's spending limits. The mechanism at the centre of the case was sponsorship. The commission found that City arranged "sham" commercial deals in which sponsors paid only part of the stated fee. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), the club's owner. On paper that looked like arm's-length commercial income. In substance it was the owner's money routed through a third party.

The ruling also covers other breaches:

- Accounts that were misstated and concealed the club's finances from auditors.
- Hidden payments that supplemented manager and player salaries.
- Failure to cooperate with the investigation. Most of the non-cooperation charges, covering 2018 to 2023, were also upheld.

The charges are therefore not only about whether a sponsor's price was too high. Related-party deals only work as a loophole if the club reports them honestly, and the commission found that City did not. Much of the league's regime rests on clubs' own declarations, and the findings suggest those declarations can be gamed for years.

## Legal status

The position is incomplete. The commission has ruled on liability, and sanctions will follow in a separate process. Possible penalties reported include a points deduction or, at the extreme, expulsion from the league. City have until Friday 2 October to appeal, and the club has said it was "disappointed and surprised" and is "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League". It has promised to be "relentless" in pursuing appeals. Reports differ on whether the club was found guilty of "all" charges or of 114 of 115. The count of 114 is the one used by NBC and CBS, and it is used here.

An appeal could take months, and the club is currently leading the league. Sporting consequences may therefore lag the legal ones by some distance.

## How football is reacting

The reaction has been bitter, and not only from rivals. Roy Keane, speaking on ITV during England's Nations League win over the Czech Republic, said the club had cheated. Some coverage has described him as a former City captain, but that is wrong. Keane captained Manchester United, City's neighbours and rivals, so his words carry a rival's edge. He directed them at the players who collected medals in the period, which included three Premier League titles.

> "They knew it would hurt a lot of people, but they still done it... if I was a player with the success of the last few years – I'd 100 per cent be sticking those medals in the bin."

That is a pundit's rhetoric, not a ruling. It does show that the argument is moving from the boardroom to the dressing room. It now concerns whether the trophies themselves have value. Other commentary has predicted a lasting stain on the era. The league has so far not said whether any titles would be affected, and nothing in the findings reported so far addresses that.

## The self-regulation problem

The case took years to reach a verdict, and the conduct it examined ended in 2018. A regulator that finds a breach eight years after the last season it covers has a problem with deterrence, however strong the eventual finding. During that time City won the league repeatedly, and any penalty will fall on a squad and a staff that may look quite different from the ones who benefited.

The design weakness is in how the system works. Clubs report their own sponsorships, and the league then has to prove that the valuations were false. The ownership can fund the "sponsor". Non-cooperation charges show what happens when a club declines to hand over the evidence.

The same structure exists in many industries that supervise themselves, including trade bodies, professional standards boards and other sporting federations. They all depend on members to disclose related-party dealings accurately. The City ruling shows that such a system can uncover abuse. It took a long time to do so, and it needed a formal process with the power to compel evidence.

Two things will show whether it works. The first is the appeal outcome. If the findings survive, the league will have established that self-regulation can hold a dominant member to account. The second is the sanction. A penalty seen as token would confirm the suspicion that the rules bind only those who lack the resources to fight them. The sanctions hearing follows the 2 October appeal deadline, and both will be watched well beyond football.
man-city-findings-fallout.in_one_sentence: An independent commission found Manchester City broke Premier League financial rules, but sanctions and appeals are pending, and the case tests whether self-regulation can police its strongest members.

women-in-trades.headline: Women take up DIY and plumbing trades as shortages bite
women-in-trades.body_md:
Britain has a plumber problem, and part of the fix is turning up in an unexpected place: the adult-education college workshop, where more women are learning to sweat a copper joint. The change is small in absolute terms. As a signal of how tight the labour market is for skilled hands, it is worth reading closely.

The starting point is a low one. Industry estimates put women at only around 1% of UK plumbers, and the shortfall of plumbers and heating engineers is put at about 59,000, according to trade-press analysis of the 2026 market. Recruitment difficulty in plumbing and heating and ventilation work is reported at roughly 23%. Those are secondary figures from industry sources, not official statistics, and should be read as indicative.

## Why the doors are opening

The demand side is not subtle. Heat-pump and decarbonisation programmes are expanding faster than the workforce that must install them. A trade that once recruited from a narrow pool of school-leavers, overwhelmingly male, now has more work than pairs of hands. When a firm cannot fill a van, the question of who is in the driving seat matters less.

Trade bodies and industry commentators have made the argument bluntly: women are an under-used pool of labour. The share of women in skilled trades has been growing in most sectors over the past decade, though from very small bases, and the pace is slow. No reliable national series yet tracks year-on-year intake by trade, which is why the anecdotes outrun the data.

## The barriers that remain

The hiring convention may be cracking, but the training pipeline has not caught up. A traditional apprenticeship can run for several years on pay at or near the apprentice minimum, which shuts out career-changers with rent to pay. Women who want to retrain in their thirties or forties, often the most motivated entrants, usually need savings or a partner's income to bridge it. Employers offering higher starting pay, or shorter conversion routes, would find a ready audience.

That is the piece the evidence does not yet show. There is no clear data that firms are paying a premium specifically to attract women, nor that hiring standards have been loosened. The more likely story is a broader one: pay for qualified tradespeople is being bid up regardless of who fills the role, and openness to new recruits is a by-product.

## What it means for pay and prices

For economists, trades are a useful barometer. Repairs, boiler installations and home improvement feed directly into household costs, and skilled-labour scarcity tends to show up first in day rates. With the Bank of England's Ramsden saying he would back rate rises if inflation persists, and gilt yields near 19-year highs, persistent wage pressure in labour-intensive services is exactly the kind of stickiness policymakers watch.

Next to watch: the Office for National Statistics' labour market release for evidence on construction vacancies and earnings, and whether government skills funding for adult retraining is widened. Without shorter routes into the trades, the shortage will keep pushing up wages, whoever holds the wrench.

huel-advert-banned.headline: Huel advert banned for suggesting products could replace all conventional food
huel-advert-banned.body_md:
A man who, by one account, eats nothing but Huel turned up at an ultramarathon and won it. That anecdote, told in a podcast-style video by the brand's ambassador, has now cost Huel an advert. The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), Britain's ad regulator, has banned the spot for encouraging or condoning "irresponsible" dietary practices.

## The ad

The video ran as a sponsored Instagram post and a YouTube pre-roll ad. It showed Spencer Matthews, the television personality and Huel ambassador, talking to Huel's founder, Julian Hearn. Matthews described meeting a competitor in a 260km race who "only eats Huel". The man, he said, "won it by miles, like literally just left us all in the dirt."

The ASA received four complaints and examined whether the ad was irresponsible.

## The ruling

The regulator accepted that the ad did not explicitly tell anyone to swap all their food for Huel. It concluded that viewers could still reasonably take the story as an endorsement. In its reading, the ad implied that replacing all conventional food with the shakes was "nutritionally appropriate" and compatible with elite physical performance.

Huel's defence was that Matthews came across as sceptical throughout. The company said he showed "extreme scepticism and disbelief" and that the anecdote was "a remarkable and unexpected occurrence, not as a recommendation." The Instagram caption also said the product was "not for every meal". The company told BBC News it had complied with the ruling.

The finding turns on the ad's overall impression rather than its literal words. A winning athlete is a strong image, and the ASA judged that it outweighed the caveat.

The triage summary for this piece framed the ruling as one about unsubstantiated claims. The published coverage instead describes a finding of irresponsibility, which is a different breach of the advertising code.

## A familiar name at the ASA

The Grocer reports that this is Huel's fifth censure by the ASA in four years. The trade title's headline describes an earlier round as over unauthorised health claims. Detail on the earlier rulings was not available for this article.

The timing is awkward for the company. Founded by Hearn in 2015, Huel sells powders, shakes and bars in what is described as a roughly $5.9bn complete-nutrition market. It is reported to be in the process of being acquired by the French food group Danone. A ruling that its marketing implies total food replacement sits uneasily beside that corporate backdrop.

## What next

Bans of this kind carry no fine. The ASA requires the ad not to appear again in its current form and expects the advertiser to take care with future campaigns. Persistent offenders can be referred to Trading Standards. The thing to watch is whether the Danone deal completes and whether its owners tighten the brand's influencer scripts. Ambassador anecdotes are where meal-replacement marketing keeps getting into trouble.

floor.body_md: The bot identified a coherent theme and executed cleanly. Nvidia's $13bn Hugging Face acquisition and disclosed $99bn AI-infrastructure portfolio caught market attention; the bot's ASML position—semiconductor-equipment supplier—captured the move directly. The 5.04% gain, banked at midday take-profit, anchored the £227.67 result. AZN.L added secondary gains. floor.headline: Clean Setups, Climactic Volume
floor.body_md:
The momentum thesis checked every box: ALK.L, GLW.DE, and RBT.MC all had price above the moving averages, positive MACD, and volume that looked like genuine demand. The bot took all three. None of them held.

The setups weren't the problem—the follow-through was. RBT.MC's volume spike reached 5.4x average, the cleanest entry of the day, but the surge collapsed without continuation. Climactic burst, not accumulation. ALK.L fared worse: sub-average volume meant the uptrend had no real conviction, and it stopped out at the full 5% loss. GLW.DE landed in between at 4.5%.

The takeaway: these trades live or die on whether that opening volume spike turns into sustained buying. When it doesn't, there's no margin for error. The setups themselves may be sound, but the confirmation signal needs more vetting. Tomorrow's momentum trades should be pickier about what passes for real demand.
